That feeling of being drunk or inebriated or tipsy or lightheaded is something that many, not all, but many humans seem to enjoy and pursue even though typically it leads to a feeling of being less happy, less motivated, more stressed, et cetera, when the alcohol wears off.
cues.zh: 但大多数人饮酒是为了改变自己的内在状态，为了获得不同于平时的感受。那种喝醉、微醺、发飘或头晕目眩的感觉，是许多人——虽然不是所有人，但确实是许多人——似乎都很享受并且去追求的，尽管在酒劲过去之后，通常会让人感到快乐减少、动力不足、压力增加等等。

cues.en: That's pretty incredible, right? I mean, we're talking about a substance that people have been highly motivated to pursue that are still highly motivated to pursue, to create and to consume, that they'll spend money on. And that's despite the fact that it makes them feel good and then it makes them feel lousy. Now, some of you might be saying, well, I drink, but I don't drink to excess and therefore I don't feel lousy. I feel good when I drink and then it wears off and it allows me to get through my evening and then the next morning I'm ready to go. Okay, that very well may be true. I believe those people.
cues.zh: 这挺不可思议的，对吧？我是说，我们谈论的是一种人们极度渴望追求、至今仍极度渴望追求、酿造、饮用并愿意为此花钱的物质。尽管它先是让你感觉良好，随后又让你感觉糟糕透顶。现在，有些人可能会说，我也喝酒，但我不过量，所以我不会觉得难受；我喝的时候感觉很好，等酒劲过了，我度过了一个美好的夜晚，第二天早上依然精力充沛。好吧，这很有可能是真的，我相信这些人说的是实话。

cues.en: And as I mentioned at the beginning of the episode, I'm not here to demonize alcohol in any way, but I do want to point out what alcohol is and how it creates the effects that it does. And then I want to talk about what those effects are when you engage in consuming alcohol, even as-
cues.zh: 正如我在本期开头提到的，我不是要妖魔化酒精，但我确实想指出酒精是什么，以及它如何产生这些影响。然后我想谈谈当你饮酒时，这些影响究竟是什么，哪怕只是——

cues.en: often is one or two nights per week. Or let's say you're just somebody who has a drink or two on Friday, maybe a few more on Saturday, or maybe you're somebody who consumes all your alcohol one night per week or one night per month. We'll talk about how that's affecting your biology. So let's address what alcohol is and how it affects the cells and tissues and organs of your body. Then we'll take a look at some of the epidemiology, that is how many people are consuming alcohol and how much they're drinking. And then you will be able, I think, to get a good sense of how the alcohol that you're drinking, if you're drinking any,
cues.zh: 通常只是每周一两个晚上。或者比如说，你只是周五喝一两杯、周六可能多喝几杯的人，或者你每周有一个晚上、每月有一个晚上把所有酒都喝掉。我们会讨论这如何影响你的生理。那么先谈谈酒精是什么，以及它如何影响你身体的细胞、组织和器官。然后我们看一些流行病学数据，也就是有多少人在饮酒、喝多少。然后我想你就能很好地了解你喝的酒精——如果你喝的话——

cues.en: at all is impacting your brain and body and the choices you might want to make about how and when to drink alcohol, or even if you want to eliminate alcohol altogether. Okay, so some basic chemistry and biology of alcohol. And again, I'll make this very clear, even if you don't have a chemistry and biology background, because of the structure of alcohol, it is what's called both water soluble and fat soluble. Translated into what's meaningful for you, what that means is when you drink alcohol, it can pass into
cues.zh: 到底如何影响你的大脑和身体，以及你可能想如何选择喝酒的方式和时机，甚至是否想完全戒酒。好，那么讲讲酒精的一些基础化学和生物学。再说一次，我会讲得很清楚，即使你没有化学和生物学背景；由于酒精的结构，它既被称为水溶性，也被称为脂溶性。换成对你有意义的说法，就是当你喝酒时，它能进入——

cues.en: all the cells and tissues of your body. It has no trouble just passing right into those cells. So unlike a lot of substances and drugs that actually attach to the surface of cells, to receptors as they're called, low parking spots, and then trigger a bunch of downstreams, like domino cascades of effects.
cues.zh: 你身体的所有细胞和组织。它能毫无困难地直接进入这些细胞。所以，不像许多物质和药物那样，实际上附着在细胞表面——也就是所谓的受体，像停车位一样——然后触发一连串下游反应，像多米诺骨牌式的效应。

cues.en: Alcohol actually has its own direct effects on cells because it can really just pass into those cells. So it's water and fat soluble. And the fact that it can pass into so many organs and cells so easily is really what explains its damaging effects. I should mention that there are three main types of alcohol. There's isopropyl, methyl and ethyl alcohol. And only the last one, ethyl alcohol or ethanol is fit for human consumption. However, it is still toxic.
cues.zh: 酒精实际上对细胞有直接影响，因为它真的能直接进入这些细胞。所以它既溶于水也溶于脂肪。而它能如此轻易地进入这么多器官和细胞，正是其破坏性影响的原因。我应该提一下，酒精主要有三种类型。异丙醇、甲醇和乙醇。只有最后一种，也就是乙醇，适合人类饮用。然而，它仍然有毒。

cues.en: It produces substantial stress and damage to cells. I'd love to be able to tell you otherwise, but that's just a fact. Ethanol produces substantial damage to cells. And it does that because when you ingest ethanol, it has to be converted into something else because it is toxic to the body. And there's a molecule inside of all of us called NAD. And you may have heard of NAD because it's quite popular. There's a lot of discussion about NAD.
cues.zh: 它会对细胞造成显著压力和损伤。我很希望能告诉你不是这样，但这就是事实。乙醇会对细胞造成显著损伤。它之所以如此，是因为当你摄入乙醇时，它必须被转化成其他东西，因为它对身体有毒。我们每个人体内都有一种叫 NAD 的分子。你可能听说过 NAD，因为它很热门，有很多关于 NAD 的讨论。

cues.en: in the longevity literature right now. NAD is present in all ourselves from birth until death. The levels of NAD tend to go down across the lifespan. There are ideas that increasing levels of NAD may extend lifespan. A lot of that is still controversial, or at least we should say is ongoing in terms of the research. But nonetheless, when you ingest ethanol, NAD and related
cues.zh: 在当下的长寿医学文献中。从出生到死亡，NAD 存在于我们所有的细胞中。随着年龄增长，NAD 水平往往会下降。有观点认为提高 NAD 水平可能会延长寿命。这很大程度上仍有争议，或者至少可以说，相关研究还在进行中。但即便如此，当你摄入乙醇时，NAD 及相关

cues.en: biochemical pathways are involved in converting that ethanol into something called acetylaldehyde. It's broken down into acetylaldehyde. And if you thought ethanol was bad, acetylaldehyde is particularly bad. Acetylaldehyde is poison. It will kill cells. It damages and kills cells. And it is indiscriminate as to which cells it damages and kills. Now,
cues.zh: 生化途径会参与将乙醇转化为一种叫做乙醛的物质。它会被分解成乙醛。如果你觉得乙醇已经够糟了，那乙醛还要糟糕得多。乙醛就是毒药。它会杀死细胞。它会破坏并杀死细胞。而且它不分青红皂白，见细胞就杀。那么，

cues.en: That's a problem, obviously. And the body deals with that problem by using another component of the NAD biochemical pathway to convert acetylaldehyde into something called acetate. Acetate is actually something that your body can use as fuel. And that process of going from ethanol to acetylaldehyde to acetate does involve the production of a toxic molecule.
cues.zh: 这显然是个问题。而身体解决这个问题的方法，是利用 NAD 生化途径的另一个组成部分，将乙醛转化为一种叫做乙酸的物质。乙酸实际上是一种身体可以用作燃料的东西。而从乙醇到乙醛再到乙酸的这个过程，确实会产生一种有毒分子。

cues.en: Right, again, acetyl aldehyde is really toxic. And NAD, and if we want to get technical, it's the NAD to NADH ratio, and that chemical step is the rate limiting step to ethanol's metabolism. What does that mean for you? What that means is that if your body can't do this conversion of ethanol to acetyl aldehyde to acetate fast enough, well, acetyl aldehyde will build up in your body and cause more damage.
cues.zh: 没错，再说一次，乙醛是真的有毒。而 NAD——如果要说得更专业一点，其实是 NAD 与 NADH 的比例——在这一步化学反应中，是乙醇代谢的限速步骤。这对你来说意味着什么？这意味着如果你的身体无法足够快地完成从乙醇到乙醛、再到乙酸的转化，那么乙醛就会在体内积聚并造成更多损害。

cues.en: it's important that your body be able to do this conversion very quickly. And the place where it does that is within the liver. And cells within the liver are very good at this conversion process, but they are cells and they are exposed to the acetaldehyde in the conversion process. And so cells within the liver really take a beating in the alcohol metabolism events. So the key thing to understand here is that
cues.zh: 所以你的身体能极快地完成这种转化至关重要。进行这一过程的地方就在肝脏。肝脏内的细胞非常擅长这种转化过程，但它们毕竟是细胞，在转化过程中同样会暴露在乙醛之下。因此，肝脏内的细胞在酒精代谢过程中确实会饱受摧残。所以这里需要理解的关键在于，

cues.en: When you ingest alcohol, you are, yes, ingesting a poison and that poison is converted into an even worse poison in your body. And some percentage of that worst poison is converted into a form of calories that you can use to generate energy, generate ATP. And the reason why alcohol is considered empty calories is because that entire process is very metabolically costly, but there's no real nutritive value of the calories that it creates.
cues.zh: 当你饮酒时，没错，你确实是在摄入一种毒药，而且这种毒药在体内还会转化为一种更可怕的毒药。这种更可怕的毒药有一部分会被转化为一种热量形式，你可以用它来产生能量、产生 ATP。酒精之所以被视为“空热量”，是因为这整个过程在代谢上代价极高，但它产生的热量却毫无真正的营养价值。

cues.en: You can use it for immediate energy, but it can't be stored in any kind of meaningful or beneficial way. It doesn't provide any vitamins. It doesn't provide any amino acids. It doesn't provide any fatty acids. It's truly empty calories. I know some people talk about sugar is empty calories, but sugar actually is a far better fuel source than alcohol or acetate. But nonetheless, when you ingest alcohol, some percentage is being shuttled into a worse poison and some is being shuttled into a fuel source.
cues.zh: 你可以用它来应急供能，但它根本无法以任何有意义或有益的方式储存起来。它不提供任何维生素。它不提供任何氨基酸。它也不提供任何脂肪酸。这才是真正的空热量。我知道有人说糖是空热量，但糖实际上是比酒精或乙酸好得多的燃料来源。但无论如何，当你饮酒时，一部分会被转化为更厉害的毒药，另一部分则被转化为燃料。

cues.en: Now, the important thing to understand is that it is the poison, the acetylaldehyde itself, that leads to the effect of being inebriated or drunk. I think most people don't realize that, that being drunk is actually a poison-induced disruption in the way that your neural circuits work. And so we should ask ourselves, which...
cues.zh: 关键要理解的是，正是这种毒物——乙醛本身——导致了醉酒或喝醉的效果。我认为大多数人没意识到，醉酒其实是毒物诱导的神经回路运作紊乱。所以我们应该问自己，哪些……

cues.en: neural circuits, what brain areas, what body areas involved in feeling drunk or inebriated. Now, in thinking about this state of being tipsy or happy or really drunk or a little bit drunk, I want to mention something I think most people aren't aware of. And that's the fact that for people that are regular drinkers or that have a genetic predisposition to alcoholism, when they drink, they tend to feel very energized and very good for longer periods of time.
cues.zh: 神经回路、哪些脑区和身体区域参与了醉酒感。现在，在思考微醺、愉悦、烂醉或有点醉这些状态时，我想提一件我认为大多数人不知道的事。那就是，对于经常饮酒的人或有酒精依赖遗传易感性的人，喝酒时往往会在更长时间里感到非常有活力、感觉很好。

cues.en: Again, people have a genetic predisposition to alcohol or people who are chronic drinkers or even just, if you recall, chronic doesn't have to mean a ton of alcohol, but they're drinking one or two per night or they're every other night type drinkers or Thursday through Sunday drinkers. Those people typically experience an increase in alertness and mood when they drink, whereas occasional drinkers will have a briefer
cues.zh: 再说，有酒精遗传易感性的人，或长期饮酒者，甚至只是——如果你还记得，长期并不一定意味着大量饮酒——但他们每晚喝一两杯，或是隔天喝一次，或是周四到周日喝的人。这些人喝酒时通常警觉性和情绪都会提升，而偶尔饮酒者会有更短暂的

cues.en: meaning less long lasting period of feeling good when they drink and then more quickly transition into a state in which they're tired or they start losing motor skills, they start slurring their speech. I also want to emphasize this is distinct from tolerance. We'll talk about tolerance later and exactly what tolerance means. But I really want to highlight the fact that when people ingest this poison, because indeed it is poison, the range of effects is very different and you can reliably predict
cues.zh: 也就是说，喝酒后感觉良好的持续时间更短，然后更快转入疲倦状态，或开始丧失运动技能，开始口齿不清。我还想强调，这与耐受性不同。我们之后会讲耐受性，以及耐受性到底意味着什么。但我真想强调，当人摄入这种毒物——因为它确实是毒物——效果范围差异很大，而且你可以可靠地预测

cues.en: Who are the people with a predisposition to alcoholism? And who are the people who are more regular drinkers by the contour, the timing of the different effects? And again, people who tend to feel more alert and excited every time they drink, they tend to get a real lift. They become kind of the life of the party and that lasts a long while. Those people are the ones that really have to be careful about predisposition for alcoholism. And those people also need to be careful about their,
cues.zh: 谁有酒精依赖的易感性？谁又是更规律的饮酒者——从不同效应的轮廓和时间进程就能看出？再说，每次喝酒都更容易感到警觉和兴奋的人，往往会获得真正的提振。他们会有点像派对气氛担当，而且这种状态持续很久。这些人正是必须特别当心酒精依赖易感性的人。这些人也需要小心自己的，

cues.en: drinking and the amount of drinking that they're doing, even if they're not full-blown alcoholics. Now, of course, people who are ingesting alcohol, who are not accustomed to drinking alcohol have to be concerned about drinking alcohol for other reasons because it can impair motor function and judgment, et cetera. But in thinking about the biochemical effects of alcohol and what it's doing to the body, what it's doing in all cases is it's consumed
cues.zh: 饮酒以及自己的饮酒量，即使他们还不是彻头彻尾的酒精依赖者。当然，摄入酒精但不习惯喝酒的人，还必须因其他原因担心饮酒，因为它会损害运动功能和判断力等等。但在思考酒精的生化效应及其对身体的作用时，它在所有情况下做的都是：它被摄入

cues.en: into the gut, right? Goes into the stomach. The liver immediately starts this conversion that we talked about before of ethanol to acetyl aldehyde to acetate. And some amount of acetyl aldehyde and acetate are making it into the brain. It crosses the blood brain barrier. Again, the brain has this fence around it that we call the blood brain barrier or the BBB. Many things.
cues.zh: 进入肠道，对吧？进入胃。肝脏立刻开始我们之前谈过的转化：乙醇变成乙醛，再变成乙酸。一部分乙醛和乙酸会进入大脑。它能穿过血脑屏障。再说，大脑周围有一道围栏，我们称之为血脑屏障，或 BBB。很多东西。

cues.en: most things, thankfully, can't pass across the blood-brain barrier, but alcohol, because it's water and fat soluble, just cruises right across this fence and into the milieu, the environment of the brain, which is made up of a couple different major cell types, neurons, nerve cells, and so-called glial cells, which are in between the nerve cells. And we'll talk about the effects on each of those soon. So what happens when alcohol gets into the brain that makes us feel tipsy or drunk, and in some people makes people feel really, especially energized and happy? Well,
cues.zh: 万幸的是，大多数物质都无法穿透血脑屏障，但酒精由于兼具水溶性和脂溶性，能直接穿过这道屏障，进入大脑内部环境；大脑主要由几种不同类型的细胞构成：神经元（即神经细胞），以及夹在神经细胞之间的所谓胶质细胞。我们稍后会讲到酒精对这两种细胞的影响。那么，酒精进入大脑后究竟发生了什么，会让我们感到微醺或喝醉，甚至让某些人感到格外兴奋和快乐呢？

cues.en: Alcohol is indiscriminate in terms of which brain areas it goes to. Again, it doesn't bind to particular receptors, but it does seem to have a propensity or an affinity for particular brain areas that are involved in certain kinds of thinking and behavior. So one of the first things that happens is that there's a slight, at least after the first drink or second drink,
cues.zh: 酒精进入大脑时并不会挑挑拣拣。再说一次，它并不与特定受体结合，但似乎确实偏好或亲和某些特定的大脑区域，而这些区域与特定思维和行为方式密切相关。因此，最先发生的事情之一，至少在喝完第一杯或第二杯酒后，

cues.en: there's a slight suppression in the activity of neurons in the prefrontal cortex. This is an area of your neocortex that's involved in thinking and planning and perhaps above all in suppression of impulsive behavior. So if you go to a party and they're serving alcohol and people are consuming drinks, what you'll notice is that a few minutes into that party, the volume of people's voices will increase.
cues.zh: 就是前额叶皮层的神经元活动会受到轻微抑制。这是新皮层中负责思考、规划，或许最重要的是负责抑制冲动行为的区域。所以，如果你去参加一个提供酒水的派对，人们一边喝酒，你就会注意到，派对开始几分钟后，大家说话的音量就会变大。

cues.en: And that's because people are simply not paying attention to their voice modulation. As other people start speaking more loudly, other people are speaking more loudly. We've all had this experience, right? Of going to a party and then you step outside for a moment and you go, oh my goodness, I was shouting. You come over the next day, you got a sore throat. Might be that you picked up some sort of bug, some virus or something. But oftentimes it's just the fact that you've been shouting all night just to be heard because as the prefrontal cortex shuts down, people stop modulating their level of speech quite as much.
cues.zh: 这是因为人们根本不再注意调节自己的音量了。随着其他人说话声音越来越大，其他人也会跟着更大声。我们都有过这种经历，对吧？去参加派对，然后走到外面透口气时，你会恍然大悟：“天哪，我刚才一直在吼啊。”第二天醒来，你嗓子哑了。这可能是染上了某种病毒或感冒，但往往只是因为你整晚都在大喊大叫好让别人听见，因为随着前额叶皮层功能的减退，人们对说话音量的调节就不那么灵敏了。

cues.en: I also noticed that people start gesticulating more, people will start standing up and sitting down more, they'll start walking around more. If there's music on, people might spontaneously start dancing. All of this is because these areas of the prefrontal cortex normally are providing what's called top-down inhibition. They are releasing a neurotransmitter called GABA onto various parts of the brain. They're involved in impulsive motor behavior and thought patterns. And as you shut down the prefrontal cortex, that GABAergic suppression of impulses
cues.zh: 我还注意到大家的手势变多了，人们会更频繁地起立又坐下，到处走动也变多了。如果放了音乐，大家可能还会自发跳起舞来。这一切都是因为前额叶皮层的这些区域平时负责所谓的“自上而下抑制”。它们会向大脑不同部位释放一种名为 GABA 的神经递质，这些部位与冲动性动作行为和思维模式相关。而当你的前额叶皮层功能受限时，那种通过 GABA 能对冲动的抑制

cues.en: starts to be released. So people will say things that they want to say without so much forethought about what they're saying, or they might do things.
cues.zh: 就会开始被打破。所以人们想到什么就说什么，不再深思熟虑，或者会直接付诸行动。

cues.en: that they want to do without really thinking it through quite as much. Or they might not even remember thinking it through at all or experience, I should say, thinking it through at all. We haven't talked about blacking out yet in the effects of alcohol on memory. But as long as we're there, I'll just tell you that alcohol has a very strong effect in suppressing the neural networks that are involved in memory formation and storage. This is why oftentimes we forget the events of a night out if we've been drinking. One of the more important things to know about the effects of alcohol in the brain
cues.zh: 做他们想做的事，却没怎么认真想清楚。或者他们甚至不记得自己认真想过，或者说，根本不记得有过认真思考这回事。在酒精对记忆的影响中，我们还没谈到断片。但既然说到这里，我就告诉你们，酒精会强烈抑制参与记忆形成和储存的神经网络。这就是为什么喝酒后，我们常常忘记晚上出去玩的经历。关于酒精对大脑的影响，更需要知道的一点是

cues.en: is this disruption in top-down inhibition, but also that areas of the brain that are involved in flexible behavior, sort of considering different options, like I could do A or I could do B. I could say this to them or I could say that. I could say it in that way or I could say it in this way. This might be a little more tactful. But since you don't know which genes you express unless you do genetic testing and those things are available, but most people aren't doing that, this assay, if you will, and it's not an assay, as we say, an assay is a test that you run in the lab to determine something.
cues.zh: 如果你的直系亲属或多位亲戚有长期酗酒史，那么你很可能会有酗酒倾向。但除非做基因检测，否则你根本不知道自己表达了哪些基因——虽然可以做检测，但大多数人并没有做——所以可以通过这种“化验”，如果你想这么叫的话，当然这不算化验，我们说的化验是指在实验室里做的检测。

cues.en: And it's not one that I recommend that you go drink in order to do. But if you've noticed that you or somebody else is somebody who can drink a lot throughout the night and have increased energy, you can just drink and drink a drink. And especially if there's blackout episodes, not remembering things the next day, despite being alert throughout the entire night and so on. Well, then I would be very concerned that you might actually have a genetic variant predisposing you to alcoholism. The other thing that predisposes people to abuse of alcohol is age. People who start drinking
cues.zh: 而且我也不建议你为了测试去喝酒。但如果你发现自己或别人能整晚大量饮酒，而且越喝越精神，一杯接一杯停不下来，特别是如果还会断片，整晚都很清醒但第二天完全想不起来等等，那我就会非常担心你可能带有易导致酗酒的基因突变。另一个导致酗酒的因素是年龄。开始饮酒

cues.en: at younger ages are greatly predisposed to developing alcohol dependence, regardless of your family history of alcoholism. Okay, so I'm going to repeat that. People who start drinking younger are at great risk for developing alcoholism, even if they don't have alcoholism in their family. Now, of course, you don't have to be an epidemiologist to understand that if you grew up in a family of drinkers and alcohol is everywhere, and especially if there's peer pressure or lack of oversight, then there's going to be a
cues.zh: 年龄较小的人，产生酒精依赖的几率要高得多，无论是否有酗酒家族史。好，我再强调一遍：即使家族中没有酗酒史，较早开始饮酒的人患酗酒症的风险也极高。当然，不需要流行病学家来解释你也明白，如果你生长在一个爱喝酒的家庭，身边到处都是酒，再加上同龄人压力或缺乏管教，那么

cues.en: higher tendency or a higher probability, I should say, that you will start drinking at a younger age. However, even people that grow up nowhere near their relatives, if they start drinking at a young age, so for instance, at 13 or younger or 14 or 15, there's a much higher probability that they're going to develop a long-lasting dependence on alcohol. People who take their first sip of alcohol later, 15, 16, or one would hope even later, I can say one would hope, because I'm now of that.
cues.zh: 你很可能会、或者说更有概率在更小的年纪就开始喝酒。然而，即使从小远离亲戚长大的人，如果他们很早就开始喝酒，比如在13岁甚至更小，或者14、15岁，他们产生长期酒精依赖的概率也会高得多。而那些较晚才喝第一口酒的人，比如15、16岁，甚至希望更晚的人——我之所以说“希望”，是因为我现在就是这种看法。

cues.en: you know, age and generation where you, you know, you think about all the things that young people do and you go, oh gosh, if they only would wait or if they only would abstain, you know, it's just what happens. I don't know. There's some neural circuit for that that I can't explain yet. But people who, for instance, drink only once they reach legal age of drinking, which in the US, I believe in every state is 21 years old. If they take their first drink at 21,
cues.zh: 到了某个年纪和代际，回顾年轻人的种种所作所为，你就会忍不住感叹：哎呀，他们要是能等等，或者忍住不碰该多好，但事情往往就是发生了。我不知道为什么，大脑里可能有某种我还无法解释的神经回路在起作用。不过，比如那些严格等到法定饮酒年龄才喝酒的人——在美国我记得各州都是21岁——如果他们21岁才喝第一口酒，

cues.en: the probability that they'll go on to develop full-blown alcohol dependence or alcohol use disorder as it's called, AUD, is very low. Now, a subset of them will because they have such a strong genetic predisposition where maybe life circumstances create a pattern in which they become a chronic drinker. But I found this very interesting. Genes matter, but also the age in which somebody starts drinking really matters. Now, whether or not that's because there are changes in neural circuitry,
cues.zh: 那么他们日后发展成重度酒精依赖，或者临床上所说的酒精使用障碍（AUD）的概率就会非常低。当然，其中有一小部分人还是会患病，这是因为他们有极强的遗传易感性，或者生活境遇导致他们形成了长期酗酒的模式。但我觉得这点很有意思：基因确实重要，但一个人开始饮酒的年龄也同样至关重要。至于是因为饮酒改变了神经回路，

cues.en: as a consequence of that drinking, then make people want to seek out more and more alcohol, or whether or not there's some other effect, maybe it's a change in hormones, et cetera, that predisposes those young drinkers to become chronic drinkers or even full-blown alcoholics, certainly developing alcohol use disorder. There's definition for that. We can talk about it. It involves the amount of drinking over a certain period of time, et cetera. So it's very clear that drinking early in life creates a propensity for
cues.zh: 从而促使人们不断寻求更多酒精，还是存在其他影响，比如激素变化等等，使得这些年轻的饮酒者更容易成为长期饮酒者、甚至完全成瘾的酗酒者，毫无疑问会发展成酒精使用障碍。对此医学上有明确的定义，我们之后可以细聊，它涉及到特定时期内的饮酒量等等。因此显而易见的是，年少时饮酒会大大增加

cues.en: the development of alcohol use disorder later in life. And while there is a genetic component to developing alcohol use disorder, I find it very interesting that if people who have those gene variants delay their onset of drinking, well, then the probability that they'll develop full blown alcohol use disorder drops as well. So again, it's genes and environments, not an either or, and there's no single gene for alcoholism. Well, I promise you, I will also talk about some of the documented
cues.zh: 日后罹患酒精使用障碍的倾向。尽管患上酒精使用障碍有基因层面的因素，但我觉得非常有意思的是，即使携带这些风险基因突变的人，只要推迟开始饮酒的年龄，他们最终患上重度酒精使用障碍的概率也会随之大幅下降。所以说，这依然是基因与环境的共同作用，绝非二选一，而且也不存在单一的酗酒基因。当然，我也向大家保证过，接下来会讲讲有据可查的

cues.en: positive effects of alcohol, although they are very few and far between, they do exist. But before I do that, I would be remiss if I didn't emphasize some more of the terrible things that alcohol does and the way that it does it. And for those of you that enjoy alcohol, again, I really like to say I feel guilty about telling you this because I know how much some people enjoy a good drink every once in a while. And I say a good drink because some people do like the taste of alcohol.
cues.zh: 酒精对人体的正面功效，尽管这种益处微乎其微且极为罕见，但确实存在。不过在此之前，如果我不进一步强调酒精带来的那些严重危害及其作用机制，那就是我的失职了。对于平时喜欢喝酒的朋友，我真的得说，告诉你们这些让我感到挺过意不去的，因为我知道偶尔小酌一杯对某些人来说有多享受。我说“小酌一杯”，是因为确实有人喜欢酒的滋味。

cues.en: I suppose I lucked out in that I don't really like the taste of alcohol and that just puts me to sleep, but I know that people do enjoy it. And I do want to point out that there is zero evidence that, you know, provided somebody is of drinking age, certainly not in the stage of brain development, that having one drink or two drinks every now and again, meaning every three or four weeks or once a month, that is not going to cause major health.
cues.zh: 我觉得自己挺幸运的，因为我并不怎么喜欢酒的味道，而且一喝就犯困，但我完全理解大家乐在其中。另外我想特别说明的是，目前没有任何证据表明，在达到法定饮酒年龄、且大脑已发育成熟的前提下，偶尔喝上一两杯——也就是每三四周或者一个月喝一次——会对健康造成什么重大危害。

cues.en: concerns or major health issues for most people. I suppose if you have zero or very little alcohol dehydrogenase, it might make you feel sick, but then you're probably not the kind of person that's going to be drinking at all. So again, if you enjoy alcoholic drinks, I'm not trying to take them away from you by any means, but you should know what drinking does if you're consuming it in this kind of typical chronic pattern as we can now refer to it, which is that one or two a night or
cues.zh: 对大多数人来说，倒不用担心会有重大健康问题。我想，如果你体内完全没有或只有极少量的乙醇脱氢酶，喝酒可能会让你感到恶心，但那样的话，你大概根本就不会去喝酒。所以再次说明，如果你喜欢喝酒，我绝不是想剥夺你的这个爱好，但如果你是以这种典型的长期饮酒模式在喝——我们现在可以这么称呼它——即每晚喝上一两杯，或者

cues.en: a few stacked up on Friday and maybe three or four on Saturday, this kind of pattern of drinking, which is quite common. And one of the more serious effects that we should think about is the impact on the so-called gut-brain axis, or for today's discussion, the gut-liver-brain axis. I don't think the gut-liver-brain axis has ever been discussed on this podcast, maybe any podcast, although the moment I say that, I'm going to, you know, the gut-liver-brain axis people are going to come after me with, I suppose, gut-liver-brain and brains. In any event,
cues.zh: 周五连着喝几杯，周六可能再来个三四杯，这种饮酒模式非常普遍，你就应该了解饮酒带来的影响。而我们需要考虑的一个更严重的后果，就是对所谓“肠-脑轴”的影响，或者以我们今天的讨论来说，是对“肠-肝-脑轴”的影响。我想在这个播客里，甚至在任何播客里，都还没讨论过肠-肝-脑轴，不过我刚说完这句话，可能研究肠-肝-脑轴的人就要端着肠、肝、脑来找我理论了。不管怎样，

cues.en: You have a brain, you have a gut, that gut runs from your throat down to the end of your intestine. Your gut and your brain communicate by way of nerve cells, neurons and nerve connections, the vagus nerve in particular, and by way of chemical signaling. Your gut also communicates by way of chemical signaling, and believe it or not, by way of neural signaling to your liver. And as we talked about earlier, the liver is the first site in which alcohol
cues.zh: 你有大脑，也有肠道，这肠道从你的喉咙一直延伸到肠道末端。你的肠道和大肠通过神经细胞、神经元和神经连接进行交流，尤其是迷走神经，同时也通过化学信号交流。你的肠道还会通过化学信号，信不信由你，还会通过神经信号与肝脏交流。正如我们之前谈到的，肝脏是酒精被分解和代谢成其各组分的第一站。

cues.en: is broken down and metabolized into its component parts. The liver is also communicating with the brain through chemical signaling and neural signaling. So we have the gut-liver-brain axis. And what you find is that people who ingest alcohol at any amount are inducing a disruption in the so-called gut microbiome, the trillions of little micro bacteria,
cues.zh: 肝脏同样通过化学信号和神经信号与大脑进行交流。所以我们有了肠-肝-脑轴。你会发现，摄入任何剂量酒精的人，都会对其所谓的肠道微生物组造成破坏，那可是数以万亿计的微小细菌，

cues.en: that take resident in your gut and that live inside you all the time and that help support your immune system and that literally signal by way of electrical signals and chemical signals to your brain to increase the release of things like serotonin and dopamine and regulate your mood generally in positive ways. Well, alcohol really disrupts those bacteria. And this should come as no surprise. I mean, earlier we talked about this and it's well known if you want to sterilize something, you want to kill the bacteria, you pour alcohol on it. And I can remember scraping my...
cues.zh: 它们定居在你的肠道里，时刻生活在你的体内，帮助支持你的免疫系统，并且实实在在地通过电信号和化学信号向你的大脑发送信号，以促进血清素和多巴胺等物质的释放，并在整体上对你的情绪起到积极的调节作用。然而，酒精确实会破坏这些细菌。这其实一点也不奇怪。我是说，我们之前就讨论过，而且大家都知道，如果你想消毒某种东西、杀死细菌，你就会往上面倒酒精。我还记得小时候擦伤……

cues.en: myself or cutting myself. I was always injuring myself when I was a kid. And, you know, the moment they take out the peroxide, you're like, oh boy, here it comes. But if there's no peroxide around and you've got a wound there and you need to clean it out, yeah, they'll use alcohol, which I do not recommend, by the way. And that's one of the harshest ways to clean a wound. But for centuries, thousands of years, really, alcohol has been used in order to clean things and kill bacteria.
cues.zh: 擦伤或割伤自己。我小时候总是弄伤自己。你知道，只要他们一拿出双氧水，你心里就会想：哎呀，又要受罪了。但如果周围没有双氧水，你身上又有伤口需要清理，是的，他们就会用酒精，顺便说一句，我并不推荐这样做。因为这是清理伤口最刺激的方式之一。但几个世纪甚至几千年来，酒精确实一直被用来清洁物品和杀灭细菌。

cues.en: alcohol kills bacteria and it is indiscriminate with respect to which bacteria it kills. So when we ingest alcohol and it goes into our gut, it kills a lot of the healthy gut microbiota. At the same time, the metabolism of alcohol in the liver, which you now understand that pathway involving NAD, acetyl aldehyde and acetate, that pathway is pro-inflammatory. So it's increasing the release of inflammatory cytokines, things like IL-6, et cetera.
cues.zh: 酒精能杀菌，而且它杀菌是不分好坏的。因此，当我们摄入酒精并进入肠道时，它会杀死大量健康的肠道微生物。与此同时，酒精在肝脏中的代谢——你们现在已经了解了涉及 NAD、乙醛和乙酸盐的代谢途径——这个途径是促炎的。所以它会增加炎性细胞因子的释放，比如 IL-6 等等。

cues.en: tumor necrosis factor alpha. If you'd like to learn more about the immune system, we did an episode all about the immune system. You can find it at ubermanlab.com. I'll teach you all the basics of what are cytokines, what are mast cells, et cetera. In any event, all these pro-inflammatory molecules, those are being released. You've now got disruption of the gut microbiota. As a consequence, the lining of the gut is disrupted and you develop, at least transiently,
cues.zh: 肿瘤坏死因子-alpha。如果你想了解更多关于免疫系统的知识，我们专门做过一期关于免疫系统的节目。你可以在 hubermanlab.com 找到。我会给你讲讲所有的基础知识，什么是细胞因子，什么是肥大细胞等等。无论如何，所有这些促炎分子都被释放出来了。此时你的肠道微生物群已经被破坏。结果就是，肠道黏膜屏障受损，你至少会暂时出现，

cues.en: leaky gut. That is bacteria that exist in the gut, which are bad bacteria can now pass out of the gut into the bloodstream. So you've got a two hit kind of model here in biology. We talk about two hit models that is kind of a one plus one equals four. And it's generally when you hear two hit, it's not a good thing. So you've got bad bacteria.
cues.zh: 肠漏症。也就是肠道里的坏细菌，现在可以穿透肠道进入血液循环。生物学上把这种现象叫做“二次打击”模型。所谓的二次打击模型，就像是一加一等于四。通常只要听到“二次打击”，就绝不是什么好事。所以现在坏细菌，

cues.en: from partially broken down food moving out of the gut. The good bacteria in the gut have been killed. You might say, why doesn't the alcohol kill the bad bacteria in the gut? Well, the bad bacteria that are from partially digested food oftentimes escape the gut before the alcohol can disrupt them. And so now you've got leaks in the gut.
cues.zh: 来自部分消化的食物中的坏细菌正在移出肠道。而肠道里的好细菌已经被杀死了。你可能会问，酒精为什么不把肠道里的坏细菌也杀死呢？这是因为，来自部分消化食物的坏细菌往往在酒精破坏它们之前就已经逃离了肠道。于是现在你的肠道就出现了渗漏。

cues.en: you've got the release of this bad bacteria, you've got inflammatory cytokines and other things being released from the liver, and they are able to get into the brain through what's called a neuro-immune signaling. And what's really bizarre in terms of the way that this manifests in the brain, I mean, it's not the way I would have done it, but then again, as I always say, I wasn't consulted at the design phase, and anyone who says they did, you should be very skeptical of them.
cues.zh: 坏细菌被释放出来，肝脏释放出炎性细胞因子和其他物质，它们能通过所谓的“神经-免疫信号通路”进入大脑。在大脑中的这种表现机制真的很诡异，要是我来设计绝不会这么搞，不过就像我常说的，设计之初可没人来征求我的意见，谁要是说被咨询过，你可千万别信。

cues.en: The net effect of this is actually to disrupt the neural circuits that control regulation of alcohol intake. And the net effect of that is increased alcohol consumption. So this is just terrible, right? I mean, so you're taking in something that disrupts two systems, the gut microbiota, and it disrupts in two ways. It's killing the good gut microbiota, and it's allowing the bad bacteria to move from the gut into the bloodstream. You've also got
cues.zh: 最终的结果实际上是破坏了调控酒精摄入的神经回路。而直接后果就是饮酒量增加。这简直太糟糕了，对吧？也就是说，你摄入的东西破坏了两个系统，首先破坏了肠道微生物群，而且是以两种方式破坏：既杀死了有益的肠道菌群，又让坏细菌从肠道溜进血液。同时你体内还有

cues.en: pro-inflammatory cytokines coming from the liver, and those converge or arrive in the brain and create a system in which the neural circuits cause more drinking. That's a bad situation. And this is why people who drink regularly, even if it's not a ton of alcohol, again, of the sorts of patterns of drinking I talked about before, and certainly for those that are chronic heavy drinkers, what you end up with is a situation in which you have inflammation in multiple places in the brain and body,
cues.zh: 来自肝脏的促炎细胞因子，它们汇聚或到达大脑，构建出一种让神经回路促使你喝得更多的机制。情况变得非常糟糕。这就是为什么经常喝酒的人——即使喝得不算特别多，就像我之前提到的那些饮酒模式，更不用说那些长期重度饮酒的人了——最终都会陷入这样一种局面：大脑和身体多处出现炎症，

cues.en: and the desire to drink even more and to further exacerbate that inflammation and the gut leakiness. So this is basically a terrible scenario for the gut liver brain axis. And it's especially prevalent in so-called alcohol use disorder. Again, people that are ingesting somewhere between 12 and 24 drinks per week. For those of you that are interested in learning more about the gut liver brain axis and in particular alcohol use disorder, I'll provide a link in the show note captions. Now there's a wonderful review on this that details that. But on the positive side,
cues.zh: 而且想喝得更多，进一步加剧炎症和肠漏。所以对于“肠-肝-脑轴”来说，这基本上是最糟糕的局面了。在所谓的“酒精使用障碍”人群中尤为普遍。再次说明，这指的是每周饮酒大约在 12 到 24 杯之间的人。如果你有兴趣深入了解肠-肝-脑轴，特别是酒精使用障碍，我会在节目简介中附上链接。有一篇非常棒的综述详细介绍了这些。但往好处看，

cues.en: it points to the possibility that at least some, again, at least some of the negative effects of alcohol consumption, whether or not you're somebody who's currently ingesting alcohol or who used to ingest alcohol and is trying to so-called repair these systems of the brain and body, whether or not replenishing the gut microbiota is going to be beneficial. And we know that there are ways to do that. And we know that there's at least some promise for the ability for the system to repair itself.
cues.zh: 这也指向了一种可能性：至少饮酒带来的某些负面影响——无论你是目前正在饮酒的人，还是曾经饮酒并试图修复大脑和身体这些系统的人——补充肠道微生物群是否会带来益处。我们知道确实有方法可以做到这一点。而且我们知道，人体系统自我修复的能力至少还是大有希望的。

cues.en: How does one do that? Well, I've talked before about this on the podcast, but studies done by colleagues of mine at Stanford, Justin Sonnenberg, who's been on this podcast as a guest, an amazing episode all about the gut microbiome, and his collaborator, Chris Garner, also at Stanford School of Medicine, have explored not alcoholism, but what are ways to improve the gut microbiota in particular to reduce the production of inflammatory cytokines.
cues.zh: 这该怎么做呢？我之前在播客里提到过，我斯坦福大学的同事 Justin Sonnenberg——他也曾作为嘉宾来过本播客，做过一期关于肠道微生态的精彩节目——以及他在斯坦福医学院的合作者 Chris Garner，他们探讨的不是酗酒本身，而是改善肠道菌群的方法，特别是如何减少炎性细胞因子的产生。

cues.en: and to adjust what's called the inflammatome. You've heard of the genome and the proteome, et cetera. Well, the inflammatome is the total array, or at least the near total array of genes and proteins that control inflammation. How can you reduce inflammation and make that inflammatome healthier? Well, they've shown that two to four servings of fermented foods per day, and here I'm not referring to fermented alcohol. I'm talking about low sugar fermented foods, so things like kimchi, sauerkraut, natto,

cues.zh: 而且我绝不想给任何人造成困惑或误导，我想强调一下这个统计数据：根据你参考的研究不同，每摄入 10 克酒精——也就是每天 10 克，相当于每天一杯酒——患癌风险就会增加 4% 到 13%，尤其是乳腺癌。但我必须强调，哪怕这相当于每周喝七杯酒，
